papers.title_in_file: Qracle: A Graph-Neural-Network-based Parameter Initializer for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, datasets, evaluation, results, conclusion
papers.what_it_is: A graph neural network that predicts initial parameters for variational quantum eigensolver circuits, compared in simulation with random and diffusion model initialization.

assertions.value: The authors report that, averaged over the validation set of each application, Qracle reduces initial loss by up to 10.86, decreases optimization steps by up to 64.42%, and reduces SMAPE by up to 26.43%, compared with state of the art initialization techniques.
quotes: Qracle achieves a reduction in initial loss of up to 10.86, accelerates convergence by decreasing optimization steps by up to 64.42%
improves final performance with up to a 26.43% reduction in Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE), with all results averaged over the validation set of each respective application
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; best case figures (up to).
assertions.reader_inference: These are best case maxima across applications, not typical gains. Per application values are in Table II (not extracted).

assertions.value: The authors report that on randomly generated VQE tasks Qracle gave only a marginal improvement in mean initial loss over the diffusion model, and that neither learned method showed a significant advantage over random parameter initialization.
assertions.anchor: Section VI-B, Random VQE Model, p.8
quotes: Overall, Qracle achieves only a marginal improvement in mean initial loss
the initial loss distributions for both Qracle and the diffusion model show no significant advantage compared to random parameter initialization
they struggle to learn effective mappings from random Hamiltonians to optimized VQE ansatz parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on generated instances.
assertions.reader_inference: The gains depend on physical structure in the Hamiltonian; the authors attribute this to missing structure but do not test that cause.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Heisenberg XYZ dataset uses 4 qubits and the Ising dataset uses 8 qubits, each with a single ansatz layer, and that each dataset is split 70% training and 30% testing.
quotes: with nq = 4 qubits and a single layer (l = 1)
with nq = 8 qubits and a single layer (l = 1)
Each dataset is split into 70% training and 30% testing
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in Section V datasets and Table I of the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Instances are small (4 to 8 qubit) simulations; scaling to larger VQE problems is not tested in the passages read.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum sequel of neural network training (Communications Physics, 2025; file name says How to Train Your Dragon)
papers.what_it_is: A scheme that uses a D-Wave quantum annealer to train a classical neural network on a subset of MNIST, with a proposed fully coherent extension that was not run.

assertions.value: The authors report a training error scaling exponent of 1.01 for quantum propagation on a D Wave annealer, against 0.78 for classical backpropagation and 0.64 for equilibrium propagation.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Results, Benchmark, p.1 and p.5
quotes: We found that this quantum training achieves superior performance scaling compared to classical backpropagation methods, with a clearly higher scaling exponent (1.01 vs. 0.78).
Blue triangles are data from the equilibrium propagation training, Eq. (5), the corresponding exponent is z = 0.64.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on a small MNIST subset network.
assertions.reader_inference: Exponent compares error decay per epoch and ignores per update cost; wall clock or energy advantage is not shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark network has a 784 neuron classical input layer, 120 hidden qubits and 40 output qubits, and uses a subset of MNIST.
quotes: Fig. 1 | NN architecture implemented on the D-Wave annealer. The input layer consists of 784 neurons
The hidden and output layers, comprised of 120 and 40 neurons respectively, are encoded as qubits on the quantum annealer.
We adopted the architecture and image dataset (a subset of MNIST) as described in ref. 53.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of its setup, Methods and Fig. 1, p.1-2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the fully coherent protocol, which they argue could double the scaling exponent, was not implemented, because the D Wave device is not expected to keep coherence over multiple forward and backward annealing runs.
quotes: Namely, it can potentially double the scaling exponent, z, in
We have not yet implemented such fully coherent protocol, since the D-Wave device is not expected to maintain coherence over multiple forward and backward runs
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own limit, p.6.

assertions.value: The authors describe their experiments as a proof of principle and list larger datasets, deeper architectures and systematic comparisons with state of the art classical approaches on more challenging tasks as future directions.
quotes: The favorable scaling observed in our proof-of-principle experiments
Future directions naturally include larger datasets, deeper architectures, and systematic comparisons with state-of-the-art classical approaches on more challenging tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope, Conclusions p.6.

papers.title_in_file: Hybrid Quantum-Classical k-Means Clustering via Quantum Feature Maps
papers.what_it_is: A k-means variant that replaces Euclidean distance with a fidelity based quantum kernel, tested on the Iris and breast cancer datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that the SU2 feature map gave an accuracy of 88.6% on Iris and 91.0% on breast cancer, and that classical k-means produced an accuracy of 83 percent on Iris.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section 4, p.1 and p.7
quotes: the SU2 feature map yielding an accuracy of 88.6% on the Iris dataset and 91.0% on the breast cancer dataset
which produced an accuracy of 83 percent
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on two small datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper is internally inconsistent: the abstract says 88.6 and 91.0, text says 88.7 and 91.0, tables give 88.67 and 91.39. The paper does not state whether runs used a simulator or hardware, or report repeated runs.

assertions.value: The authors report that the ARI and AMI scores of the EfficientSU2 feature map are better than those of classical k-means on both datasets.
quotes: The table shows that the ARI and AMI scores of the EfficientSU2 feature map are better than those of classical K-means in both datasets, indicating that the quantum algorithms perform better.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Differences in the tables are small (for example 0.6407 against 0.6348 ARI on breast cancer) and no variance is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that Iris has 150 samples and 4 features and breast cancer has 569 samples and 10 features, using 4 qubits for Iris and 10 qubits for breast cancer.
quotes: The Iris dataset contains 150 samples, 4 numerical features, and 3 species, while the Breast Cancer dataset contains 10 features and 569 samples.
We will be using 4 qubits for the Iris dataset, which matches the number of features.
For the Breast Cancer dataset, we will be using 10 qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup, Section 3.2, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that misclassifications persist, particularly where the original data classes overlap.
quotes: While misclassifications persist, particularly in regions where the original data classes overlap
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own limit, p.8.

papers.title_in_file: Pulsed learning for quantum data re-uploading models
papers.what_it_is: A pulse level version of a data re-uploading quantum neural network, compared in noisy simulation with its gate based counterpart.

assertions.value: The authors report that in simulation the pulse based model outperformed its gate based counterpart in test accuracy and generalization under equivalent noise, and kept useful accuracy at depolarizing probabilities where the gate based model had degraded to near random performance.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section IV, p.1 and p.9-10
quotes: The pulse-based model consistently outperforms its gate-based counterpart, exhibiting higher test accuracy and improved generalization under equivalent noise conditions.
the pulse-based model retains useful classification accuracy at depolarizing probabilities where its gate-based counterpart has already degraded to near-random performance
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Simulated device, two qubits only; no hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results come from numerical simulation of two qubit configurations, benchmarked under noise extracted from the IBM Brisbane device, on four binary classification tasks, with all experiments repeated over five random seeds.
assertions.anchor: Sections I and IV-A, p.2 and p.8
quotes: benchmark it under realistic noise extracted from the IBM Brisbane device
across four distinct binary classification tasks (MNIST digits, Iris, Corners, and Helix)
we restrict our analysis to two-qubit configurations
All experiments are repeated over five different random seeds.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup, Sections I and IV-A.

assertions.value: The authors state two main limitations: computational cost restricted the simulations to two qubit systems, and the encoding stage remains gate based.
quotes: First, computational cost restricted our simulations to two-qubit systems
Second, the encoding stage remains gate-based in the present work
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own limits, Section V.

assertions.value: The authors note that the depolarizing probabilities explored exceed typical single gate error rates and describe them as a controlled stress test.
quotes: We note that the depolarizing probabilities explored here exceed typical single-gate error rates
they provide a controlled stress test that reveals relative robustness differences
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope, Section IV-C.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Hamiltonian Evolution for Coherent Quantum Learning
papers.partial_detail: abstract, main text including numerical demonstrations and conclusion; supplement skimmed by headings only
papers.what_it_is: A proposed training framework in which model parameters are quantum degrees of freedom evolved under a Hamiltonian that encodes the loss, demonstrated numerically on toy problems.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical experiments on binary classification and interferometric phase estimation show the evolved probability distribution peaking at the optimal parameters.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Numerical demonstrations, p.1 and p.5
quotes: Numerical experiments on binary classification and interferometric phase estimation confirm that the evolved distribution peaks at the optimal parameters, matching gradient-based performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study on toy problems.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract also says the result matches gradient based performance; the main text numerical section does not show such a comparison (the supplement was not read in full).

assertions.value: The authors state that the classification demonstration uses a single qubit data re-uploading circuit with two layers of trainable rotations and two parameters, each discretized with five qubits, for one training epoch.
quotes: we employ a single-qubit data reuploading circuit with two layers of trainable rotations, yielding a variational ansatz with two parameters
Each parameter is then discretized using five qubits.
we perform one training epoch using the coherent training protocol in the single-sample regime
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup, p.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that a complete complexity analysis is beyond the scope of the work and that whether coherent learning can give asymptotic advantages over hybrid optimization is an open question.
quotes: While a complete complexity analysis is beyond the scope of this work
Determining whether coherent learning can provide asymptotic advantages over hybrid optimization remains an important open question.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own limit, p.5.

papers.title_in_file: Practical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Radar Micro-Doppler Classification on NISQ Hardware
papers.partial_detail: whole paper through the comparative analysis; references skipped
papers.what_it_is: A quantum kernel SVM applied to simulated radar micro-Doppler data, run in a simulator and on IBM Torino and IBM Fez, compared with a classical RBF SVM.

assertions.value: The authors report on simulated radar data that a classical RBF SVM reached 98.52% accuracy with 15 features and the QSVM simulator reached 94.81% with 4 PCA features.
quotes: The Classical SVM achieves a slightly higher accuracy of 98.52% by utilizing all 15 extracted micro-Doppler features. In contrast, the QSVM attains a competitive accuracy of 94.81% while operating with only 4 features obtained through PCA-based dimensionality reduction.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on simulated data.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical SVM was more accurate; the QSVM figure is for the simulator, not hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report an estimated fidelity of approximately 89% on IBM Torino and 94% on IBM Fez for the measured output distributions, and state that Fez outperforms Torino in fidelity, entropy and noise resilience.
quotes: IBM Fez consistently outperforms IBM Torino in fidelity, entropy and noise resilience.
Higher fidelity: An increase from approximately 89% to 94% reflects more accurate execution of quantum operations and improved state preparation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a distribution fidelity on one circuit, not a classification accuracy on hardware; the paper does not report hardware classification accuracy in the passages read.

assertions.value: The authors state that the data are simulated: a 9 GHz X band radar with three aerial target classes and 450 samples, 150 per class.
quotes: a simulated 9 GHz (X-band) radar system was employed with the following parameters
The dataset contains 450 samples, with each class containing 150 samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup, Sections 4.1 and 4.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dominant QSVM cost lies in quantum kernel estimation, which is significantly slower than classical kernel computation, and that QSVM does not currently provide an overwhelming speed advantage.
quotes: the dominant cost in QSVM lies in quantum kernel estimation, which is significantly slower than classical kernel computation.
Thus, QSVM does not currently provide an overwhelming speed advantage
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own limit, Section 6.1.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 9 of the same paper lists QSVM as faster in training, which sits uneasily with this statement.

papers.title_in_file: Support Vector Machine with a Scalable Quantum Kernel
papers.what_it_is: A classical post processing method (Hamming quantum kernel) for quantum kernel SVMs that avoids exponential concentration, evaluated in simulation up to 27 qubits.

assertions.value: The authors report that in simulations with 2 to 27 qubits the Hamming quantum kernel outperformed the fidelity quantum kernel whenever 15 or more qubits were used.
quotes: using systems ranging from 2 to 27 qubits
Throughout the simulations, the Hamming quantum kernel outperforms the fidelity quantum kernel whenever 15 or more qubits are used.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Compared on MNIST subsets and one synthetic set only.

assertions.value: The authors report that on synthetic data generated from quantum circuits the Hamming quantum kernel consistently outperformed the classical Gaussian kernel.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section V-B, p.1 and p.10
quotes: Furthermore, for synthetic quantum data, our method consistently outperforms the classical Gaussian kernel.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The data were generated by quantum circuits, so a quantum kernel advantage there does not show an advantage on classical or real world data.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the MNIST 0 versus 6 task the classical RBF kernel had the best test accuracy for all qubit counts.
quotes: Fig. 3(b) shows the test accuracies for the different kernels for the 0 vs. 6 classification task. The classical RBF kernel exhibits the best classification accuracy for all values of n.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: On classical data the paper's own result shows no quantum kernel advantage over the RBF baseline.

assertions.value: The authors state that the MNIST 0 and 6 dataset has 100 training and 99 test samples, and the quantum circuit dataset has 100 training and 100 test samples.
assertions.anchor: Sections V-A2 and V-B, p.8 and p.10
quotes: This dataset also consists of 100 training and 99 test samples, comprising digits 0 and 6.
The dataset consists of 100 training samples and 100 test samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup.
assertions.reader_inference: Small test sets limit the precision of accuracy comparisons.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum vs. Classical Machine Learning: A Benchmark Study for Financial Prediction
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, setup, results for directional classification, live trading and volatility, conclusion
papers.what_it_is: A benchmark comparing simulated quantum neural networks, QLSTMs and quantum SVR with architecture matched classical models on equity direction, trading and volatility tasks.

assertions.value: The authors report that hybrid quantum neural networks surpass the parameter matched ANN by +3.8 AUC and +3.4 accuracy points on AAPL and by +4.9 AUC and +3.6 accuracy points on the Turkish stock KCHOL.
quotes: In directional classification, hybrid quantum neural networks surpass the parameter-matched ANN by +3.8 AUC and +3.4 accuracy points on AAPL stock and by +4.9 AUC and +3.6 accuracy points on Turkish stock KCHOL.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulated study, final walk forward fold.
assertions.reader_inference: Results refer to the final test slice (fold 5) of a walk forward split; no significance test is quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors state that all quantum models are executed in simulation using statevector simulation with exact expectation values.
quotes: All quantum models are executed in simulation mode.
Quantum circuits are evaluated using statevector simulation with exact expectation values.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware noise or shot cost is included.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the seven feature cross asset equity experiment the classical ANN achieved higher AUC and accuracy than the QNNs, and conclude that classical models keep an advantage on mid range cross asset features.
assertions.anchor: Section V-B and Conclusion, p.16 and p.19
quotes: the classical ANNs model performs slightly better than QNNs with the ANNs achieving higher AUC and accuracy
At the same time, classical models retain an advantage on mid-range cross-asset features
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulated study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in a live trading simulation across four market regimes of the S&P 500, the QLSTM improved risk adjusted returns in two regimes and underperformed economically in the post pandemic regime.
quotes: we assessed both LSTM and QLSTM models in a live trading simulation across four distinct market regimes of the S&P 500
QLSTM improves riskadjusted returns in two of four market regimes
QLSTM underperforms economically
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical backtest from one simulated study.
assertions.reader_inference: Mixed result: gains in two regimes, a loss in at least one; the authors note high sensitivity to threshold choice.
